primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Pathogenic SI variants reduce brush-border sucrase-isomaltase activity, impairing digestion of sucrose and portions of starch and producing osmotic gastrointestinal symptoms after exposure to these carbohydrates.
vignette: An 18-month-old girl has recurrent watery diarrhea, abdominal distention, and bloating that began after fruit, table sugar, and starch-containing foods were introduced into her diet. She tolerates lactose-containing foods. Small-bowel biopsy shows preserved villous architecture, but mucosal disaccharidase testing shows markedly reduced sucrase and isomaltase activities.
lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
distractors: Cystic fibrosis with pancreatic exocrine insufficiency
distractor_notes: Primary lactase deficiency causes symptoms after lactose exposure; this child tolerates lactose and has selectively reduced sucrase/isomaltase activity.
Celiac disease causes an immune-mediated enteropathy with villous injury rather than preserved villous architecture with selective brush-border sucrase-isomaltase deficiency.
Pancreatic insufficiency causes fat and protein maldigestion with steatorrhea and does not selectively eliminate mucosal sucrase/isomaltase activity.
Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth can cause bloating and diarrhea but does not explain selective severe deficiency of the sucrase-isomaltase enzyme complex on mucosal assay.
key_expl: Congenital sucrase-isomaltase deficiency is caused by deficient brush-border sucrase-isomaltase activity. Symptoms typically emerge when sucrose- and starch-containing foods are introduced and include watery diarrhea, abdominal pain/distention, and bloating. Mucosal disaccharidase testing can confirm reduced sucrase/isomaltase activity.
objective: Recognize congenital sucrase-isomaltase deficiency from carbohydrate-triggered diarrhea with preserved villous architecture and selective low sucrase/isomaltase activity.
clues: symptoms after sucrose and starch introduction
